My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 68.2 is anchored heavily to the most recent observed value, assuming mean-reverting behavior and no major catalysts expected within the next 24 hours. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 68.5 reflects a mild positive drift assumption, perhaps tied to underlying trend momentum or a slightly bullish baseline expectation. By one month, the estimate rises to 69.0, incorporating a longer-run trend component while acknowledging that the series has historically shown gradual upward pressure over multi-week periods. In each case, the point estimate is essentially a weighted blend of recent levels, short-term momentum, and a long-run mean or trend anchor.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding nature of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 2.4 units on each side, consistent with typical short-run volatility. By one week, that spread grows to roughly 5 units in each direction, and by one month it expands to 10 units — a natural consequence of uncertainty accumulating as more trading sessions, data releases, and potential regime shifts enter the picture. The key drivers of interval width include realized volatility in the underlying series, sensitivity to macroeconomic news flow, and the degree to which the series can be pulled by external shocks that are inherently unpredictable beyond a short window.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic conditions — such as a sharp rise in unemployment claims, a banking stress event, or a geopolitical escalation — could push the one-month outcome well below 59. On the upside, a surprise policy pivot, stronger-than-expected economic data, or a sentiment-driven rally could push the series above 79. The one-day interval is the most vulnerable to being breached by a single large news event, such as a major central bank announcement or an unexpected data print that arrives outside consensus expectations. Liquidity conditions and market microstructure effects could also contribute to short-lived but sharp moves that technically violate even wide confidence bounds.

If the underlying data-generating process has shifted — for instance, if there has been a structural break in the series that my model has not yet fully incorporated — then all three intervals could be systematically miscalibrated in the same direction.
